### GRI 302 Energy  
In 2025, HSBC reduced its total energy consumption by 34.5% compared with the 2019 baseline [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_132]. This reduction was driven by strategic divestments and the adoption of energy conservation programmes, supported by enhanced metering and monitoring technologies [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_132]. In the same year, 94.2% of HSBC’s electricity was sourced from renewable sources — a key milestone toward its 2030 ambition of 100% renewable electricity across its own operations [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_132][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_135]. The Group follows RE100 principles, prioritising power purchase agreements (PPAs) to procure additional renewable capacity where feasible; in markets where PPAs are unavailable (e.g., France and parts of India), it procures renewable electricity via utility partners or energy attribute certificates [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_132].

### GRI 303 Water  
HSBC states that, “taking into account the nature of our business, we do not consider [water sourcing and efficiency] to be a material issue for our stakeholders” [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1068]. Nevertheless, it reports having implemented measures to reduce water consumption, including installation of water-efficient taps and flow restrictors, and continues to track water consumption [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1068]. No quantitative water consumption data (e.g., cubic metres or litres per FTE) or targets are disclosed in the provided context.

### GRI 305 Emissions  
HSBC’s scope 1 and 2 emissions (energy and road fleet) were 36,617 tonnes CO₂e in 2025 — representing a 91.2% reduction from the 2019 baseline and a 62.9% reduction from 2024 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_135]. Scope 2 market-based emissions alone were 19,919 tonnes CO₂e in 2025, down from 392,270 tonnes CO₂e in 2019 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_137]. Scope 2 location-based emissions in 2025 were 259,129 tonnes CO₂e [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_138]. Scope 3 category 6 (business travel) emissions fell to 67,019 tonnes CO₂e in 2025 — a 75.4% reduction versus 2019 and 49.9% versus 2024 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_135][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_136]. Total scope 1, 2 and 3 (categories 1, 2 and 6) emissions were 1,076,917 tonnes CO₂e in 2025 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_138]. The Group reports scope 3 emissions using the GHG Protocol’s spend-based methodology, applying data quality scoring and third-party limited assurance for 2025 data [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_136][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_137]. For financed emissions (scope 3 category 15), HSBC discloses on-balance sheet financed emissions for in-scope target sectors, representing ~3.5% of loans and advances to customers at 31 December 2024 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1072]. Its oil and gas portfolio achieved a 38% absolute reduction in combined on-balance sheet financed and facilitated emissions versus 2019 (28.5 Mt CO₂e in 2024) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_116][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_113].

### GRI 306 Waste  
HSBC states it “does not consider hazardous waste to be a material issue for our stakeholders” and therefore reports only on total waste produced (hazardous and non-hazardous combined) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1068]. However, no quantitative data on total waste volume (e.g., tonnes), composition, recycling rates, or diversion metrics are provided in the source material [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1068].

### TCFD Strategy, Risk Management, Metrics & Targets  
HSBC’s climate strategy is anchored in its Net Zero Transition Plan, updated in November 2025, which sets commercially grounded, sector-specific financed emissions targets aligned with IEA APS and NZE 2024 scenarios [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_65][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_88]. It employs a suite of climate scenarios—including Below 2°C (Paris-aligned), Current Commitments (planning base case), and Downside Physical Risk—underpinned by NGFS, IPCC and IEA frameworks [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_540]. Climate risk is integrated into financial reporting via impairment testing, where observable climate impacts are reflected in discount rates and asset prices [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_957]. However, the company acknowledges it does not yet fully disclose the amount or percentage of assets vulnerable to physical or transition risks across wholesale/retail lending, equity/debt holdings, or trading positions — nor the metrics used to assess those impacts by industry, geography, credit quality or tenor [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1072]. It also states it does not fully describe climate-related risks and opportunities affecting cash flows, access to finance or cost of capital over short-, medium- and long-term horizons [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1068].

### Not covered in source material  
- Quantitative water consumption data (volume, intensity, or targets).  
- Total waste volumes (hazardous and non-hazardous), recycling/diversion rates, or waste management practices beyond general commitments.  
- Detailed scope 3 category disclosures beyond categories 1, 2 and 6 (e.g., employee commuting, end-of-life treatment of sold products, use of sold products).  
- Assurance level or scope for scope 1 and 2 emissions (only scope 3 category 6 and supply chain data are noted as subject to limited assurance in 2025) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_138].  
- Methodology or data for scope 1 emissions beyond the uplift rate adjustment for refrigerant leaks [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_135].

### GRI 403 Occupational Health & Safety  
HSBC reported 10 major injuries to employees in 2025, defined as fractures, dislocations, concussions, loss of consciousness, or overnight hospital admission [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_746]. The all-injury rate stood at 96 per 100,000 employees in 2025, down from 91 in 2024 and 110 in 2023 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_746]. Lost days due to work injury totalled 331 in 2025, compared with 335 in 2024 and 594 in 2023 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_746]. No workplace fatalities were recorded in 2025, 2024, or 2023, as indicated by a zero rate per 100,000 employees across all three years [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_746]. HSBC also reported that in 2025, 33 named storms affected 2,222 buildings globally, with no injuries or operational impact reported [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_746].

### GRI 404 Training  
In 2025, HSBC colleagues completed 5.6 million training hours, a decrease from 6.2 million in 2024 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_160]. This equated to 26.8 training hours per full-time equivalent (FTE) employee in 2025, down from 29.6 hours per FTE in 2024 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_160]. Mandatory conduct training was completed by 99% of employees in 2025 (and 2024) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_66]. HSBC launched the Digital Acceleration Programme in 2024, delivering over 25,000 hours of targeted training for key roles such as product owners and scrum masters by 2025 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_160]. Additionally, over 42,000 digital credentials were issued in 2025 across data, digital, banking, finance, and wealth domains, supported by 46 newly launched digital badges [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_158]. Directors received tailored training mirroring employee mandatory modules, covering risk management, operational resilience, health and safety, well-being, cyber-security, financial crime, AI, and data protection [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_604].

### GRI 405 Diversity  
At year-end 2025, women held 34.7% of senior leadership roles globally, against a publicly stated ambition of 35% [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_146][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_66]. Black heritage colleagues represented 3.0% of senior leadership roles in the UK and US combined, versus an ambition of 3.4% [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_146][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_66]. The Inclusion Index score—measured via the Snapshot employee engagement survey—reached 78% in 2025, exceeding the 75% ambition [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_146][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_66]. Of the global workforce, 69.1% voluntarily self-identified their ethnic background in 2025 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_147]. On the HSBC Holdings Board, 62% of members were women and six (46%) identified as from an ethnic minority background as of 31 December 2025 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_588].

### GRI 414 Supplier Social Assessment  
By end-2025, 97.3% of approximately 9,830 contracted suppliers had either confirmed adherence to HSBC’s refreshed Supplier Code of Conduct (which now includes principles on responsible AI use) or provided an alternative code accepted by HSBC’s Global Procurement function [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_179][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_168]. HSBC continued human rights audits of suppliers and closed out findings from 2024 audits [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_166]. Its Global Procurement function implemented a human rights due diligence operating procedure to identify higher-risk suppliers and mitigate associated risks [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_166].

### TCFD Strategy (social impacts of climate transition)  
The context does not disclose HSBC’s assessment of the social impacts—such as workforce transitions, community vulnerability, or just transition planning—arising from its climate transition strategy. While HSBC references “building inclusion and resilience” as part of its ESG ambitions [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_66], and notes stakeholder consultations on “developing issues, including the potential social impacts of AI on communities” [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_166], no specific analysis, metrics, or initiatives related to the social dimensions of climate transition (e.g., reskilling for green jobs, community investment in fossil-fuel-dependent regions, or supply chain labour impacts from decarbonisation) are reported.

### Not covered in source material  
GRI 403: Occupational health and safety policy scope (e.g., coverage of contractors, temporary workers, or outsourced staff); occupational health metrics beyond injury rates (e.g., mental health incidents, stress-related absences, or wellness programme participation).  
GRI 404: Breakdown of training hours by topic, gender, ethnicity, or seniority; expenditure on training; or verification of training effectiveness.  
GRI 405: Representation data for other underrepresented groups (e.g., LGBTQ+, disability, age); pay equity analysis or gender/ethnicity pay gaps; or detailed progress on intersectional inclusion goals.  
GRI 414: Percentage of Tier 1 or Tier 2 suppliers assessed for social criteria; number or nature of non-compliance incidents; or supplier capacity-building initiatives.  
TCFD Strategy: Disclosure of climate transition-related social risks in scenario analysis; workforce transition plans aligned with net-zero targets; or community engagement on climate adaptation/resilience programmes.

### Board Independence and Composition  
The Nomination & Corporate Governance Committee, acting on delegated authority from the Board, assessed and confirmed the independence of all non-executive Directors and the Group Chairman who stood for election or re-election at the 2025 Annual General Meeting (AGM) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_731]. This determination followed consideration of all circumstances likely to impair, or appear to impair, independence, in accordance with the UK and Hong Kong Corporate Governance Codes [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_732]. Non-executive Directors are appointed for an initial three-year term and typically serve two consecutive terms (six years), after which any further appointment is subject to a rolling one-year term and rigorous review against the Board’s evolving needs [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_731]. All Directors standing for election or re-election at the 2025 AGM were elected or re-elected by shareholders [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_731].

### Conflicts of Interest Management  
HSBC maintains an annually reviewed policy and set of procedures to manage Directors’ conflicts of interest effectively [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_732]. Directors are required to notify the Board of any actual or potential conflicts and update the Board on changes to relevant facts or circumstances [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_732]. They must review and confirm their own and their closely associated persons’ outside interests and appointments twice yearly [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_733]. All conflicts are recorded in a formal register, and the Board has authorised conflicts as they arose during 2025 in accordance with its policy and the Companies Act 2006 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_732]. Non-executive Directors undergo triennial re-vetting by the Group’s compliance team, including refreshed conflict checks [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_733].

### Anti-Corruption and Financial Crime Governance  
HSBC’s global financial crime policy explicitly prohibits bribery and corruption, requiring all activity to be reasonable, transparent, appropriately documented, and authorised at an appropriate seniority level [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_174]. Risk-based due diligence and ongoing monitoring are applied to customers and third parties to mitigate bribery and corruption risks [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_175]. In 2025, no concluded legal cases regarding bribery or corruption were brought against HSBC or its employees [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_175]. A total of 99% of permanent and non-permanent employees completed mandatory financial crime training, including anti-bribery and corruption content, in 2025 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_175].

### Climate and ESG Governance Structure  
The Group Board holds overall supervisory responsibility for ESG strategy, overseeing executive management on development, execution, and reporting [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_529]. The Group Risk Committee, chaired by James Forese, oversees ESG-related risks, including climate risk [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_165]. The Group Chief Risk and Compliance Officer is the senior manager responsible for climate risk under the UK Senior Managers Regime [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_529]. Climate risk appetite is embedded within the Group’s overarching risk appetite statement, approved and overseen by the Board, and reviewed annually or sooner if breached [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_530]. Climate risk indicators are reported quarterly to the Group Risk Management Meeting and Group Risk Committee [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_530].

### Whistleblowing and Speak-Up Mechanisms  
HSBC operates the global whistleblowing channel HSBC Confidential, which received 1,100 concerns for investigation in 2025 (2024: 925), with 34% found to have some level of substantiation [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_175]. The Group Audit Committee oversees the effectiveness of the whistleblowing framework [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_175]. Colleagues’ confidence to speak up about poor behaviour was measured at 81% in 2025 via the Snapshot employee survey [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_153].

### Not covered in source material  
Specific disclosures on board committee meeting frequency and attendance rates; detailed breakdown of director remuneration linked to ESG metrics beyond the stated inclusion in incentive scorecards; quantitative data on board diversity beyond gender and Black heritage representation at senior leadership level; explicit TCFD-aligned governance disclosures on oversight of scenario analysis assumptions or model validation processes; and verification status of anti-corruption controls by external auditors.

### GRI 302 Energy  
In 2025, HSBC reduced its total energy consumption by 34.5% compared with the 2019 baseline [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_132]. This reduction was driven by strategic divestments and the adoption of energy conservation programmes, supported by enhanced metering and monitoring technologies [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_132]. In the same year, 94.2% of HSBC’s electricity was sourced from renewable sources — a key milestone toward its 2030 ambition of 100% renewable electricity across its own operations (GRI 302-2) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_132][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_135]. The Group follows RE100 principles, prioritising power purchase agreements (PPAs) to procure additional renewable capacity where feasible; in markets where PPAs are unavailable (e.g., France and parts of India), it procures renewable electricity via utility partners or energy attribute certificates [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_132].

### GRI 303 Water  
HSBC states that, “taking into account the nature of our business, we do not consider [water sourcing and efficiency] to be a material issue for our stakeholders” [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1068]. It reports having implemented measures to reduce water consumption, including installation of water-efficient taps and flow restrictors, and continues to track water consumption [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1068]. However, no quantitative data on water withdrawal (e.g., cubic metres), breakdown by source (surface, groundwater, municipal), intensity (m³/FTE), or water efficiency targets are disclosed in the provided context [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1068]. Therefore, disclosures required under GRI 303-2 (water sources) and GRI 303-3 (water consumption targets) are not covered.

### GRI 305 Emissions  
HSBC’s scope 1 and 2 emissions (energy and road fleet) were 36,617 tonnes CO₂e in 2025 — representing a 91.2% reduction from the 2019 baseline and a 62.9% reduction from 2024 (GRI 305-2) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_135]. Scope 2 market-based emissions alone were 19,919 tonnes CO₂e in 2025, down from 392,270 tonnes CO₂e in 2019 — a 94.9% reduction [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_137]. Scope 2 location-based emissions in 2025 were 259,129 tonnes CO₂e; no baseline or 2024 value is provided for this metric [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_138]. Scope 3 category 6 (business travel) emissions fell to 67,019 tonnes CO₂e in 2025 — a 75.4% reduction versus 2019 and 49.9% versus 2024 (GRI 305-2) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_135][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_136].  

The figure of 1,076,917 tonnes CO₂e cited for “Scope 1, 2 and 3 (Category 1, 2 and 6)” in 2025 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_138] is internally inconsistent with the sum of disclosed components: scope 1 (16,698 tCO₂e) + scope 2 market-based (19,919 tCO₂e) + scope 3 category 1 (807,293 tCO₂e) + category 2 (165,988 tCO₂e) + category 6 (67,019 tCO₂e) = 1,076,917 tCO₂e [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_137]. Thus, the total reflects categories 1, 2, and 6 *plus* scope 1 and scope 2 — not scope 1+2+6 alone — and is correctly labelled as “Scope 1, 2 and 3 (Category 1, 2 and 6)” [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_138]. All 2025 scope 1, 2 and 3 (categories 1, 2, 6) data are subject to independent third-party limited assurance in accordance with ISAE 3000 / ISAE 3410 (GRI 305-2) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_138]. Scope 1 emissions include an adjustment for refrigerant leaks in cooling systems, reflected in an updated uplift rate [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_135][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_136]. For financed emissions (scope 3 category 15), HSBC discloses on-balance sheet financed emissions for in-scope target sectors, representing approximately 3.5% of loans and advances to customers at 31 December 2024 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1072]. Its oil and gas portfolio achieved a 38% absolute reduction in combined on-balance sheet financed and facilitated emissions versus 2019 (28.5 Mt CO₂e in 2024) (GRI 305-2) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_116][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_113].

### GRI 306 Waste  
HSBC states it “does not consider hazardous waste to be a material issue for our stakeholders” and therefore reports only on total waste produced (hazardous and non-hazardous combined) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1068]. However, no quantitative data on total waste volume (tonnes), hazardous vs. non-hazardous breakdown, recycling rates, diversion rates, or waste management practices are provided in the source material [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1068]. Consequently, disclosures required under GRI 306-2 (total waste generated, by type) and GRI 306-3 (waste diversion rate) are absent.

### TCFD Strategy, Risk Management, Metrics & Targets  
HSBC’s climate strategy is anchored in its Net Zero Transition Plan, updated in November 2025, which sets commercially grounded, sector-specific financed emissions targets aligned with IEA APS and NZE 2024 scenarios (TCFD Strategy) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_65][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_88]. It employs a suite of climate scenarios—including Below 2°C (Paris-aligned), Current Commitments (planning base case), and Downside Physical Risk—underpinned by NGFS, IPCC and IEA frameworks (TCFD Risk Management) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_540]. Climate risk is integrated into financial reporting via impairment testing, where observable climate impacts are reflected in discount rates and asset prices (TCFD Metrics & Targets) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_957]. However, the company acknowledges it does not fully disclose the amount or percentage of assets vulnerable to physical or transition risks across wholesale/retail lending, equity/debt holdings, or trading positions — nor the metrics used to assess those impacts by industry, geography, credit quality or tenor (TCFD Risk Management) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1072]. It also states it does not fully describe climate-related risks and opportunities affecting cash flows, access to finance or cost of capital over short-, medium- and long-term horizons (TCFD Metrics & Targets) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1068].

### Not covered in source material  
- Quantitative water consumption data (volume in m³, intensity in m³/FTE, or breakdown by source per GRI 303-2).  
- Total waste volumes (tonnes), hazardous vs. non-hazardous breakdown, recycling/diversion rates, or waste management practices beyond general commitments (GRI 306-2, GRI 306-3).  
- Full scope 3 inventory covering all 15 categories per GHG Protocol; only categories 1 (purchased goods and services), 2 (capital goods), and 6 (business travel) are disclosed [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1072][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_137].  
- Scope 1 emissions disaggregated by source (e.g., natural gas, diesel, refrigerants) with methodology notes.  
- Assurance level or scope for scope 1 and 2 emissions beyond the stated limited assurance for scope 3 categories 1, 2 and 6 and associated scope 1 and 2 components in the 2025 total [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_138].  
- Baseline year and value for scope 2 location-based emissions, or comparison to 2024 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_138].  
- Water efficiency targets (GRI 303-3).

### GRI 403 Occupational Health & Safety  
In 2025, HSBC recorded 10 major injuries to employees—defined as fractures, dislocations, concussions, loss of consciousness, or overnight hospital admission—compared with 14 in 2024 and 12 in 2023 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_746]. The all-injury rate was 96 per 100,000 employees in 2025, an increase from 91 in 2024 and a decrease from 110 in 2023 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_746]. Lost days due to work injury totalled 331 in 2025, down from 335 in 2024 and 594 in 2023 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_746]. No workplace fatalities occurred in 2025, 2024, or 2023, as reflected by a zero fatality rate per 100,000 employees across all three years [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_746]. The reporting of 33 named storms affecting 2,222 buildings in 2025—with no injuries or operational impact—reinforces HSBC’s enterprise-wide approach to physical climate risk mitigation and underpins its occupational health and safety framework by validating the resilience of its infrastructure against extreme weather events [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_746].

### GRI 404 Training  
HSBC colleagues completed 5.6 million training hours in 2025, a reduction from 6.2 million in 2024 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_160]. This represented 26.8 training hours per full-time equivalent (FTE) employee in 2025, down from 29.6 hours per FTE in 2024 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_160]. The decline reflects operational adjustments—including the transfer of certain Operations staff from Corporate Centre to business segments during 2025—which altered FTE allocation methodology and may have affected aggregated training hour calculations [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_865][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_204]. Mandatory conduct training was completed by 99% of employees in 2025 (and 2024) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_66]. The Digital Acceleration Programme—launched in 2024—delivered over 25,000 hours of targeted training for product owners and scrum masters by 2025 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_160]. Over 42,000 digital credentials were issued in 2025 across data, digital, banking, finance, and wealth domains, supported by 46 newly launched digital badges [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_158]. Directors received training aligned with mandatory employee modules, covering health and safety, well-being, cyber-security, financial crime, AI, and data protection [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_604].

### GRI 405 Diversity  
HSBC’s publicly stated 2025 ambitions—set against a 2021 baseline—were to achieve 35% representation of women and 3.4% representation of Black heritage colleagues in senior leadership roles (UK/US combined), alongside an Inclusion Index score of 75% [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_146]. By 31 December 2025, women held 34.7% of senior leadership roles globally, and Black heritage colleagues held 3.0% of such roles in the UK/US combined cohort [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_146][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_66]. The Inclusion Index score reached 78%, exceeding the 75% ambition [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_146][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_66]. Progress was constrained in 2025 by a reduction in promotions and new hires, which impacted both gender and ethnic representation targets [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_147]. Voluntary self-identification of ethnic background was provided by 69.1% of colleagues in 2025 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_147]. On the HSBC Holdings Board, 62% of members were women and six (46%) identified as from an ethnic minority background as of 31 December 2025 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_588].

### GRI 414 Supplier Social Assessment  
By end-2025, 97.3% of approximately 9,830 contracted suppliers had either confirmed adherence to HSBC’s refreshed Supplier Code of Conduct—which now includes principles on responsible AI use—or provided an alternative code accepted by HSBC’s Global Procurement function [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_179][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_168]. HSBC’s Global Procurement function implemented a human rights due diligence operating procedure to identify suppliers with higher human rights risk exposure and mitigate associated impacts [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_166]. Human rights audits of suppliers were continued in 2025, with findings from 2024 audits closed out [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_166].

### TCFD Strategy (social impacts of climate transition)  
The context does not disclose HSBC’s assessment of the social impacts arising from its climate transition strategy—including workforce transitions, community vulnerability, or just transition planning. While HSBC states “building inclusion and resilience” as an ESG ambition [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_66], and notes stakeholder consultations on “developing issues, including the potential social impacts of AI on communities” [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_166], no specific analysis, metrics, or initiatives related to the social dimensions of climate transition (e.g., reskilling for green jobs, community investment in fossil-fuel-dependent regions, or supply chain labour impacts from decarbonisation) are reported. HSBC’s TCFD disclosures focus on financed emissions, sustainable finance targets, and climate scenario analysis for credit risk—but omit dedicated treatment of social risks and opportunities linked to the transition [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1070][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1071].

### Not covered in source material  
GRI 403: Occupational health and safety policy scope beyond permanent employees (e.g., coverage of contractors, temporary workers, or outsourced staff); mental health metrics (e.g., stress-related absences, counselling uptake, or wellness programme participation); or baseline year and target for zero work-related fatalities.  
GRI 404: Training expenditure; breakdown of training hours by topic, gender, ethnicity, or seniority; or independent verification of training effectiveness (e.g., pre/post-assessments, behavioural change metrics).  
GRI 405: Gender and ethnic pay gap data (per GRI 405-21); representation data for LGBTQ+, disability, or age groups; or post-2025 diversity targets (e.g., 2027 or 2030 goals).  
GRI 414: Percentage of Tier 1 or Tier 2 suppliers assessed for social criteria; number or nature of non-compliance incidents; supplier capacity-building initiatives; or audit findings by geography or sector.  
TCFD Strategy: Disclosure of climate transition-related social risks in scenario analysis; workforce transition plans aligned with net-zero targets (e.g., reskilling pathways for employees in carbon-intensive sectors); or community engagement on climate adaptation/resilience programmes.

Governance.draft:
### Board Independence and Composition  
The Nomination & Corporate Governance Committee, acting on delegated authority from the Board, assessed and confirmed the independence of all non-executive Directors and the Group Chairman who stood for election or re-election at the 2025 Annual General Meeting (AGM) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_731]. This determination followed consideration of all circumstances likely to impair, or appear to impair, independence, in accordance with the UK and Hong Kong Corporate Governance Codes [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_732]. Non-executive Directors are appointed for an initial three-year term and typically serve two consecutive terms (six years), after which any further appointment is subject to a rolling one-year term and rigorous review against the Board’s evolving needs [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_731]. All Directors standing for election or re-election at the 2025 AGM were elected or re-elected by shareholders [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_731].

### Board Committee Meeting Frequency and Attendance  
In 2025, the Board of Directors held 7 meetings, with the Group Chairman attending all 7 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_594]. The Group Audit Committee held 6 meetings (all attended by Brendan Nelson), the Nomination & Corporate Governance Committee held 8 meetings (7 attended), the Group Remuneration Committee held 8 meetings (6 attended), the Group Risk Committee held 6 meetings (all attended by Brendan Nelson), and the Group Technology & Operations Committee held 6 meetings (5 attended) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_594]. Average attendance across all Board and committee meetings in 2025 was not aggregated in the source; however, individual attendance rates are disclosed per director and committee [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_594].

### Conflicts of Interest Management  
HSBC maintains an annually reviewed policy and set of procedures to manage Directors’ conflicts of interest effectively [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_732]. Directors are required to notify the Board of any actual or potential conflicts and update the Board on changes to relevant facts or circumstances [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_732]. They must review and confirm their own and their closely associated persons’ outside interests and appointments twice yearly [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_733]. All conflicts are recorded in a formal register, and the Board has authorised conflicts as they arose during 2025 in accordance with its policy and the Companies Act 2006 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_732]. Non-executive Directors undergo triennial re-vetting by the Group’s compliance team, including refreshed conflict checks [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_733].

### Anti-Corruption and Financial Crime Governance  
HSBC’s global financial crime policy explicitly prohibits bribery and corruption, requiring all activity to be reasonable, transparent, appropriately documented, and authorised at an appropriate seniority level [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_174]. Risk-based due diligence and ongoing monitoring are applied to customers and third parties to mitigate bribery and corruption risks [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_175]. In 2025, no concluded legal cases regarding bribery or corruption were brought against HSBC or its employees [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_175]. A total of 99% of permanent and non-permanent employees completed mandatory financial crime training, including anti-bribery and corruption content, in 2025 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_175]. The source does not disclose the 2024 training completion rate, nor the reasons for the 1% non-completion [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_175].

### Climate and ESG Governance Structure  
The Group Board holds overall supervisory responsibility for ESG strategy, overseeing executive management on development, execution, and reporting [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_529]. The Group Risk Committee, chaired by James Forese, oversees ESG-related risks, including climate risk [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_165]. The Group Chief Risk and Compliance Officer is the senior manager responsible for climate risk under the UK Senior Managers Regime [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_529]. Climate risk appetite is embedded within the Group’s overarching risk appetite statement, approved and overseen by the Board, and reviewed annually or sooner if breached [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_530]. Climate risk indicators are reported quarterly to the Group Risk Management Meeting and Group Risk Committee [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_530]. The source states that the Board “regularly reflects on the evolving nature of financial and non-financial climate risks in the real world to improve the integration of climate risk factors into strategic planning, transactions, and decision-making” but does not specify how the Board reviews or challenges underlying assumptions and methodologies used in climate scenario analyses [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_527].

### Whistleblowing and Speak-Up Mechanisms  
HSBC operates the global whistleblowing channel HSBC Confidential, which received 1,100 concerns for investigation in 2025 (2024: 925), with 34% found to have some level of substantiation [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_175]. The Group Audit Committee oversees the effectiveness of the whistleblowing framework [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_175]. Colleagues’ confidence to speak up about poor behaviour was measured at 81% in 2025 via the Snapshot employee survey [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_153]. The source does not disclose the 2024 Snapshot result for speak-up confidence [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_153].

### Executive Remuneration Linkage to ESG Metrics  
ESG metrics are included in the incentive scorecards of the Group CEO, Group CFO, and Group Operating Committee members, underpinning some of the ESG metrics reported in the Annual Report [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_66]. For the 2026 annual incentive, strategic measures (30% weighting) include customer satisfaction (15%), organisational change delivery (10%), and people and culture (5%) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_672]. The long-term incentive (LTI) for 2026–2028 includes a sustainable finance and investment measure (10% weighting) and a financed emissions measure, both tied to the $750bn–$1tn 2030 sustainable financing ambition and the Financed Emissions Metric Pathway [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_674]. However, the source does not quantify the percentage of total executive remuneration (fixed + variable + LTI) explicitly tied to measurable ESG targets such as GHG reduction or financial crime incident rates [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_66].

### Board Diversity Targets  
The Board recognises the importance of gender, social and ethnic diversity [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_614]. While the source reports that 34.7% of senior leadership roles were held by women in 2025 (2024: 34.6%) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_66], and that the Board’s diversity and inclusion policy was updated in December 2025 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_614], it does not disclose a time-bound, quantified target for representation of underrepresented groups *on the Board itself* (e.g., % women or ethnic minorities by a specified year) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_614].

### Not covered in source material  
Specific disclosures on board committee meeting frequency and attendance rates beyond the counts provided (e.g., average attendance rate across committees); detailed breakdown of director remuneration explicitly tied to measurable ESG targets (e.g., % of total pay linked to GHG reduction, financial crime incident rate, or substantiated whistleblowing case resolution time); explicit TCFD-aligned governance disclosures on how the Board reviews and challenges underlying assumptions and methodologies used in climate scenario analyses; verification status of anti-corruption controls by external auditors; the 2024 Snapshot survey result for speak-up confidence; the 2024 financial crime training completion rate; a time-bound, quantified target for representation of underrepresented groups *on the Board*; qualitative summary of root causes identified in substantiated whistleblowing cases; disclosure of whether any board-level ESG governance targets (e.g., climate risk indicator thresholds) were breached in 2025; and explanation of the reasons for the 1% non-completion of financial crime training.

### GRI 302 Energy  
In 2025, HSBC reduced its total energy consumption by 34.5% compared with the 2019 baseline [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_132]. This reduction was driven by strategic divestments and the adoption of energy conservation programmes, supported by more detailed and automated metering and monitoring [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_132]. In 2025, 94.2% of HSBC’s electricity was sourced from renewable sources — a key milestone toward its ambition to purchase 100% renewable electricity across its own operations by 2030 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_132][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_135]. The Group follows RE100 principles, prioritising power purchase agreements (PPAs) where feasible; in markets where regulation or energy profiles preclude PPAs (e.g., France and regions of India), it procures renewable electricity through utility partners or energy attribute certificates [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_132]. No quantitative data on absolute energy consumption (kWh), intensity (kWh/FTE), or breakdown by fuel type (e.g., grid electricity, natural gas, diesel) is provided beyond the aggregate percentage reduction and renewable electricity share [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_132].

### GRI 303 Water  
HSBC states: “taking into account the nature of our business, we do not consider [sourcing water issue and water efficiency target] to be a material issue for our stakeholders” [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1068]. It reports having implemented measures to reduce water consumption — including installation of water-efficient taps and flow restrictors — and continues to track water consumption [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1068]. However, the context provides **no quantitative data** on water withdrawal (e.g., cubic metres), water intensity (m³/FTE), breakdown by source (surface, groundwater, municipal), or water efficiency targets [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1068]. Therefore, disclosures required under GRI 303-1 (water withdrawal), GRI 303-2 (water sources), and GRI 303-3 (water consumption targets) are absent.

### GRI 305 Emissions  
HSBC’s scope 1 and 2 emissions (energy and road fleet) were 36,617 tonnes CO₂e in 2025 — representing a 91.2% reduction from the 2019 baseline and a 62.9% reduction from 2024 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_135]. Scope 2 market-based emissions alone were 19,919 tonnes CO₂e in 2025, down from 392,270 tonnes CO₂e in 2019 — a 94.9% reduction [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_137]. Scope 2 location-based emissions in 2025 were 259,129 tonnes CO₂e; **no baseline year value or 2024 figure is disclosed**, preventing trend analysis as required under GRI 305-2 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_138]. Scope 3 category 6 (business travel) emissions fell to 67,019 tonnes CO₂e in 2025 — a 75.4% reduction versus 2019 and 49.9% versus 2024 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_135][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_136].  

The total for “Scope 1, 2 and 3 (Category 1, 2 and 6)” is reported as 1,076,917 tonnes CO₂e in 2025, consistent with the sum of disclosed components: scope 1 (16,698 tCO₂e) + scope 2 market-based (19,919 tCO₂e) + scope 3 category 1 (807,293 tCO₂e) + category 2 (165,988 tCO₂e) + category 6 (67,019 tCO₂e) = 1,076,917 tCO₂e [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_137][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_138]. All 2025 data for this aggregated total — including associated scope 1 and scope 2 components — are subject to independent third-party limited assurance in accordance with ISAE 3000 / ISAE 3410 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_138]. Scope 1 emissions include an adjustment for refrigerant leaks in cooling systems, reflected in an updated uplift rate [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_135][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_136]. For financed emissions (scope 3 category 15), HSBC discloses on-balance sheet financed emissions for in-scope target sectors, representing approximately 3.5% of loans and advances to customers at 31 December 2024 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1072]. Its oil and gas portfolio achieved a 38% absolute reduction in combined on-balance sheet financed and facilitated emissions versus 2019 (28.5 Mt CO₂e in 2024) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_116][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_113].

### GRI 306 Waste  
HSBC states it “does not consider hazardous waste to be a material issue for our stakeholders” and therefore reports only on total waste produced (hazardous and non-hazardous combined) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1068]. It confirms continuing focus on “the reduction and recycling of all waste”, aligned with its ‘reduce, replace, remove’ environmental approach [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1068]. However, the context provides **no quantitative data** on total waste volume (tonnes), hazardous vs. non-hazardous breakdown, recycling rates, diversion rates, or waste management practices [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1068]. Therefore, disclosures required under GRI 306-2 (total waste generated, by type) and GRI 306-3 (waste diversion rate) are absent.

### TCFD Strategy, Risk Management, Metrics & Targets  
HSBC’s climate strategy is anchored in its Net Zero Transition Plan, updated in November 2025, which sets commercially grounded, sector-specific financed emissions targets aligned with IEA APS and NZE 2024 scenarios (TCFD Strategy) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_65][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_88]. It employs a suite of climate scenarios—including Below 2°C (Paris-aligned), Current Commitments (planning base case), and Downside Physical Risk—underpinned by NGFS, IPCC and IEA frameworks (TCFD Risk Management) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_540]. Climate risk is integrated into financial reporting via impairment testing, where observable climate impacts are reflected in discount rates and asset prices (TCFD Metrics & Targets) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_957]. However, HSBC explicitly states it does **not fully disclose** the amount or percentage of assets or business activities vulnerable to climate-related physical and transition risks across wholesale/retail lending, equity/debt holdings, or trading positions — nor the metrics used to assess those impacts by industry, geography, credit quality or tenor [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1072]. It also states it does **not fully describe** climate-related risks and opportunities affecting cash flows, access to finance or cost of capital over short-, medium- and long-term horizons [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1068].

### Not covered in source material  
- Absolute water withdrawal (m³), intensity (m³/FTE), or breakdown by source (surface, groundwater, municipal) per GRI 303-1 and GRI 303-2.  
- Total waste generated (tonnes), disaggregated by hazardous/non-hazardous, and recycling/diversion rates per GRI 306-2 and GRI 306-3.  
- Full scope 3 inventory covering all 15 GHG Protocol categories; only categories 1 (purchased goods and services), 2 (capital goods), and 6 (business travel) are disclosed [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1072][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_137].  
- Scope 2 location-based emissions for 2019 and 2024, required to enable comparative trend analysis per GRI 305-2 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_138].  
- Quantitative metrics on % of assets vulnerable to physical or transition risk across lending, equity, debt, or trading portfolios, segmented by sector and geography, as required under TCFD Risk Management [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1072].  
- Contribution of strategic divestments (e.g., MWh or tCO₂e avoided) to the 34.5% energy reduction [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_132].  
- Assurance scope or level for scope 1 and 2 emissions separately from the limited assurance applied to the aggregated “Scope 1, 2 and 3 (Category 1, 2 and 6)” total [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_138].

### GRI 403 Occupational Health & Safety  
In 2025, HSBC recorded 10 major injuries to employees—defined as fractures, dislocations, concussions, loss of consciousness, or overnight hospital admission—compared with 14 in 2024 and 12 in 2023 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_746]. The all-injury rate was 96 per 100,000 employees in 2025, an increase from 91 in 2024 and a decrease from 110 in 2023 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_746]. Lost days due to work injury totalled 331 in 2025, down from 335 in 2024 and 594 in 2023 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_746]. No workplace fatalities occurred in 2025, 2024, or 2023, as reflected by a zero fatality rate per 100,000 employees across all three years [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_746]. The reporting of 33 named storms affecting 2,222 buildings in 2025—with no injuries or operational impact—reinforces HSBC’s enterprise-wide approach to physical climate risk mitigation and underpins its occupational health and safety framework by validating the resilience of its infrastructure against extreme weather events [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_746].

### GRI 404 Training  
HSBC colleagues completed 5.6 million training hours in 2025, a reduction from 6.2 million in 2024 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_160]. This represented 26.8 training hours per full-time equivalent (FTE) employee in 2025, down from 29.6 hours per FTE in 2024 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_160]. The decline reflects operational adjustments—including the transfer of certain Operations staff from Corporate Centre to business segments during 2025—which altered FTE allocation methodology and may have affected aggregated training hour calculations [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_865][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_204]. Mandatory conduct training was completed by 99% of employees in 2025 (and 2024) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_66]. The Digital Acceleration Programme—launched in 2024—delivered over 25,000 hours of targeted training for product owners and scrum masters by 2025 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_160]. Over 42,000 digital credentials were issued in 2025 across data, digital, banking, finance, and wealth domains, supported by 46 newly launched digital badges [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_158]. Directors received training aligned with mandatory employee modules, covering health and safety, well-being, cyber-security, financial crime, AI, and data protection [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_604].

### GRI 405 Diversity  
HSBC’s publicly stated 2025 ambitions—set against a 2021 baseline—were to achieve 35% representation of women and 3.4% representation of Black heritage colleagues in senior leadership roles (UK/US combined), alongside an Inclusion Index score of 75% [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_146]. By 31 December 2025, women held 34.7% of senior leadership roles globally, and Black heritage colleagues held 3.0% of such roles in the UK/US combined cohort [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_146][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_66]. The Inclusion Index score reached 78%, exceeding the 75% ambition [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_146][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_66]. Progress was constrained in 2025 by a reduction in promotions and new hires, which impacted both gender and ethnic representation targets [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_147]. Voluntary self-identification of ethnic background was provided by 69.1% of colleagues in 2025 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_147]. On the HSBC Holdings Board, 62% of members were women and six (46%) identified as from an ethnic minority background as of 31 December 2025 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_588].

### GRI 414 Supplier Social Assessment  
By end-2025, 97.3% of approximately 9,830 contracted suppliers had either confirmed adherence to HSBC’s refreshed Supplier Code of Conduct—which now includes principles on responsible AI use—or provided an alternative code accepted by HSBC’s Global Procurement function [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_179][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_168]. HSBC’s Global Procurement function implemented a human rights due diligence operating procedure to identify suppliers with higher human rights risk exposure and mitigate associated impacts [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_166]. Human rights audits of suppliers were continued in 2025, with findings from 2024 audits closed out [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_166].

### TCFD Strategy (social impacts of climate transition)  
The context does not disclose HSBC’s assessment of the social impacts arising from its climate transition strategy—including workforce transitions, community vulnerability, or just transition planning. While HSBC states “building inclusion and resilience” as an ESG ambition [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_66], and notes stakeholder consultations on “developing issues, including the potential social impacts of AI on communities” [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_166], no specific analysis, metrics, or initiatives related to the social dimensions of climate transition (e.g., reskilling for green jobs, community investment in fossil-fuel-dependent regions, or supply chain labour impacts from decarbonisation) are reported. HSBC’s TCFD disclosures focus on financed emissions, sustainable finance targets, and climate scenario analysis for credit risk—but omit dedicated treatment of social risks and opportunities linked to the transition [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1070][260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_1071].

### Not covered in source material  
GRI 403: Occupational health and safety policy scope beyond permanent employees (e.g., coverage of contractors, temporary workers, or outsourced staff); mental health metrics (e.g., stress-related absences, counselling uptake, or wellness programme participation); or baseline year and target for zero work-related fatalities.  
GRI 404: Training expenditure; breakdown of training hours by topic, gender, ethnicity, or seniority; or independent verification of training effectiveness (e.g., pre/post-assessments, behavioural change metrics).  
GRI 405: Gender and ethnic pay gap data (per GRI 405-21); representation data for LGBTQ+, disability, or age groups; or post-2025 diversity targets (e.g., 2027 or 2030 goals).  
GRI 414: Percentage of Tier 1 or Tier 2 suppliers assessed for social criteria; number or nature of non-compliance incidents; supplier capacity-building initiatives; or audit findings by geography or sector.  
TCFD Strategy: Disclosure of climate transition-related social risks in scenario analysis; workforce transition plans aligned with net-zero targets (e.g., reskilling pathways for employees in carbon-intensive sectors); or community engagement on climate adaptation/resilience programmes.

### Board Independence and Composition  
The Nomination & Corporate Governance Committee, acting on delegated authority from the Board, assessed and confirmed the independence of all non-executive Directors and the Group Chairman who stood for election or re-election at the 2025 Annual General Meeting (AGM) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_731]. This determination followed consideration of all circumstances likely to impair, or appear to impair, independence, in accordance with the UK and Hong Kong Corporate Governance Codes [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_732]. Non-executive Directors are appointed for an initial three-year term and typically serve two consecutive terms (six years), after which any further appointment is subject to a rolling one-year term and rigorous review against the Board’s evolving needs [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_731]. All Directors standing for election or re-election at the 2025 AGM were elected or re-elected by shareholders [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_731].

### Conflicts of Interest Management  
HSBC maintains an annually reviewed policy and set of procedures to manage Directors’ conflicts of interest effectively [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_732]. Directors are required to notify the Board of any actual or potential conflicts and update the Board on changes to relevant facts or circumstances [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_732]. They must review and confirm their own and their closely associated persons’ outside interests and appointments twice yearly [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_733]. All conflicts are recorded in a formal register, and the Board has authorised conflicts as they arose during 2025 in accordance with its policy and the Companies Act 2006 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_732]. Non-executive Directors undergo triennial re-vetting by the Group’s compliance team, including refreshed conflict checks [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_733].

### Anti-Corruption and Financial Crime Governance  
HSBC’s global financial crime policy explicitly prohibits bribery and corruption, requiring all activity to be reasonable, transparent, appropriately documented, and authorised at an appropriate seniority level [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_174]. Risk-based due diligence and ongoing monitoring are applied to customers and third parties to mitigate bribery and corruption risks [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_175]. In 2025, no concluded legal cases regarding bribery or corruption were brought against HSBC or its employees [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_175]. A total of 99% of permanent and non-permanent employees completed mandatory financial crime training, including anti-bribery and corruption content, in 2025 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_175]. The 2024 training completion rate was also 99% [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_175]. The source does not specify the reasons for the 1% non-completion in either year [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_175]. Internal audit coverage of financial crime controls is overseen by the Group Audit Committee, which received regular updates from Global Internal Audit and expressed satisfaction with the effectiveness of the Global Internal Audit function, including its work on financial crime risk [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_626]. However, the source does not disclose whether anti-corruption controls specifically underwent external assurance or independent validation in 2025 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_626].

### Climate and ESG Governance Structure  
The Group Board holds overall supervisory responsibility for ESG strategy, overseeing executive management on development, execution, and reporting [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_529]. The Group Risk Committee, chaired by James Forese, oversees ESG-related risks, including climate risk [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_165]. The Group Chief Risk and Compliance Officer is the senior manager responsible for climate risk under the UK Senior Managers Regime [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_529]. Climate risk appetite is embedded within the Group’s overarching risk appetite statement, approved and overseen by the Board, and reviewed annually or sooner if breached [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_530]. Climate risk indicators are reported quarterly to the Group Risk Management Meeting and Group Risk Committee [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_530]. The source states that the Board “regularly reflects on the evolving nature of financial and non-financial climate risks in the real world to improve the integration of climate risk factors into strategic planning, transactions, and decision-making” but does not specify whether this reflection includes dedicated Board sessions, independent challenge functions, or third-party validation of scenario assumptions [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_527]. The source does not disclose whether any Board-approved climate risk indicator thresholds were approached or breached in 2025, nor any remedial actions taken [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_530].

### Whistleblowing and Speak-Up Mechanisms  
HSBC operates the global whistleblowing channel HSBC Confidential, which received 1,100 concerns for investigation in 2025 (2024: 925), with 34% found to have some level of substantiation [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_175]. The Group Audit Committee oversees the effectiveness of the whistleblowing framework [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_175]. Colleagues’ confidence to speak up about poor behaviour was measured at 81% in 2025 via the Snapshot employee survey [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_153]. The source does not disclose the 2024 Snapshot result for speak-up confidence [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_153]. The source reports that 793 cases raised in 2025 related to bullying and harassment, of which 30% were either partly or fully substantiated; however, it does not provide a thematic summary of root causes (e.g., process gaps, supervision failures, cultural factors) identified across substantiated whistleblowing cases [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_153].

### Executive Remuneration Linkage to ESG Metrics  
ESG metrics are included in the incentive scorecards of the Group CEO, Group CFO, and Group Operating Committee members, underpinning some of the ESG metrics reported in the Annual Report [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_66]. For the 2026 annual incentive, strategic measures (30% weighting) include customer satisfaction (15%), organisational change delivery (10%), and people and culture (5%) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_672]. The long-term incentive (LTI) for 2026–2028 includes a sustainable finance and investment measure (10% weighting) and a financed emissions measure, both tied to the $750bn–$1tn 2030 sustainable financing ambition and the Financed Emissions Metric Pathway [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_674]. The $750bn–$1tn ambition was announced in 2020, with cumulative progress since 1 January 2020 reported as $495.6bn as of 2025 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_95]. The financed emissions pathway is aligned with the 2030 target, but the source does not disclose the baseline year or starting value for the Financed Emissions Metric Pathway [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_674]. The source does not quantify the percentage of total executive remuneration (fixed + variable + LTI) explicitly tied to measurable ESG targets such as GHG reduction or financial crime incident rates [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_66].

### Board Diversity Targets  
The Board recognises the importance of gender, social and ethnic diversity [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_614]. While the source reports that 34.7% of senior leadership roles were held by women in 2025 (2024: 34.6%) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_66], and that the Board’s diversity and inclusion policy was updated in December 2025 [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_614], it does not disclose a time-bound, quantified target for representation of underrepresented groups *on the Board itself* (e.g., % women or ethnic minorities by a specified year) [260225-annual-report-and-accounts-2025 (1)_chunk_614].

### Not covered in source material  
Verification status of anti-corruption controls by external auditors or independent assurance providers (GRI 205-3); explicit disclosure of how the Board reviews and challenges underlying assumptions and methodologies used in climate scenario analyses (TCFD Governance c.1.a); disclosure of whether any board-level ESG governance targets (e.g., climate risk indicator thresholds) were breached in 2025 (TCFD Governance c.1.b); thematic summary of root causes identified in substantiated whistleblowing cases; explanation of the reasons for the 1% non-completion of financial crime training; baseline year and starting value for the Financed Emissions Metric Pathway; time-bound, quantified target for representation of underrepresented groups *on the Board* (e.g., 40% women by 2027); quantitative climate risk indicator value for 2025 and its 2024 baseline (e.g., % of portfolio aligned with 1.5°C scenarios); and whether any Board-approved climate risk indicator thresholds were approached or breached in 2025.
